strengths: Substantial real-world evaluation: The paper reports over 2,000 real-robot rollouts on an advanced bimanual humanoid platform (Unitree H1-2) with dexterous hands (Inspire hands equipped with 1,062 tactile points per hand). Real-world robotic validation at this scale is rigorous and commendable.

Valuable dataset contribution: DECO-50 provides 50 hours, 5 million frames, and over 8,000 successful trajectories across 4 multi-stage scenarios with active binocular vision, high-density tactile sensing, and bimanual dexterous coordination.

Parameter-efficient tactile adaptation: The plugin adapter enables incorporating tactile cues into a pretrained visuomotor policy by fine-tuning only ~7.97M parameters (<10% of total weights), achieving performance comparable to training from scratch with tactile inputs (DECO.ds).

Informative ablation studies: The paper provides clear ablations validating the decoupled design. Specifically, the pathway swap experiment (Table 7) convincingly demonstrates that AdaLN is better suited for global proprioceptive vectors while cross-attention is crucial for spatially localized, sparse tactile features.

Comprehensive supplementary analysis: The authors control for encoder capacity by providing ResNet-18 vs. ResNet-34 experiments (Appendix B.3), demonstrating that performance differences over baselines are not merely artifacts of visual encoder size.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core modeling choices—using joint attention for image-action tokens, AdaLN for continuous states/timesteps, and cross-attention/LoRA adapters for auxiliary conditioning—closely reflect existing practices in multimodal diffusion transformers (e.g., MMDiT/SD3) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

Confounding factors in baseline comparisons: The performance gap between DECO and DP/ACT may stem largely from the modern transformer backbone and rectified flow formulation rather than the multimodal decoupling alone. Comparing against a standard Transformer-based Diffusion Policy (e.g., Diffusion Policy with DiT / Chi et al. / Octo-style backbones) without decoupling would have better isolated the benefit of the proposed architectural decoupling.

Single-embodiment scope: All experiments and dataset recordings are carried out on a single robot embodiment and tactile sensor setup (piezoresistive array). As acknowledged in the limitations, it remains unclear how well the adapter generalizes across diverse tactile modalities (e.g., optical tactile sensors such as GelSight/Digit) or different robotic hands.

Missing public artifact links during review: Placeholders for the project page, codebase, and dataset are left empty on page 1 and page 16, preventing direct verification of reproducibility during the review phase.

strengths: Extensive and rigorous real-world evaluation involving over 2,000 physical robot rollouts across four diverse bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks on an upper-body humanoid platform (Unitree H1-2 with 6-DOF dexterous hands).

Principled architectural design that decouples conditioning pathways according to the characteristics of each modality: vision-action joint self-attention, low-dimensional proprioceptive states via AdaLN, and sparse contact tactile cues via cross-attention.

Insightful ablation experiments that explicitly validate the proposed decoupled routing: swapping tactile and proprioceptive conditioning pathways causes a catastrophic drop on contact-rich assembly (e.g., Stage 3 success drops from 29/40 to 0/40), and naive coupled injection (DECO.cs) clearly underperforms decoupled cross-attention.

Parameter-efficient tactile adaptation: the plug-in tactile adapter trains only 7.97M parameters (<10% of total model capacity) while matching the performance of models trained from scratch with tactile inputs.
Release of the DECO-50 dataset, contributing 50 hours and over 8,000 successful trajectories of bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing and active vision.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is primarily an engineering synthesis of established components (Diffusion Transformers, AdaLN, cross-attention adapters, LoRA, and rectified flow matching) tailored for visuo-tactile bimanual manipulation.
Out-of-distribution and generalizability evaluations are relatively narrow, tested only on a few unseen objects in the material sorting task.

The baseline comparison against ACT and DP conflates backbone architecture differences (Transformer + Flow Matching vs. U-Net/Transformer + DDIM/noise scheduling); while the ResNet-18 vs. ResNet-34 ablations in Appendix B.3 help, isolating the transformer backbone advantages from the decoupled conditioning could be emphasized earlier in the main text.

strengths: Extensive and rigorous real-world evaluation consisting of over 2,000 physical robot rollouts across four diverse bimanual dexterous manipulation scenarios on a full humanoid dual-arm platform (Unitree H1-2 with multi-taxel Inspire dexterous hands).

Principled and well-motivated architecture: the decoupled conditioning design in MMDiT (vision via joint self-attention, proprioception via AdaLN, and tactile via cross-attention) is empirically validated, notably through architectural ablations demonstrating that permuting modality pathways catastrophically degrades performance on contact-rich assembly.

Parameter-efficient tactile adaptation: the proposed plug-in adapter leverages LoRA and specialized tactile pooling/projection to update fewer than 10% of model parameters (~7.97M out of ~91M) while matching the performance of models trained from scratch with full fine-tuning.

Insightful empirical task analysis: the paper cleanly delineates weakly tactile-relevant tasks (where visual and proprioceptive inputs suffice) from strongly tactile-dependent tasks (where touch is critical for handling visual occlusions and force modulation), providing clear guidelines for robotic data collection.

Valuable community artifact: the release of DECO-50 provides 50 hours of bimanual dexterous manipulation trajectories paired with dense multi-taxel tactile feedback and active vision, filling an important gap in open manipulation datasets.
weaknesses: Platform and sensor specificity: the study is restricted to a single dual-arm setup with a specific piezoresistive normal-force tactile sensor array, leaving unverified how well the decoupled architecture and adapter generalize across different tactile modalities (e.g., optical tactile sensors like GelSight or high-frequency dynamic tactile sensors).

Limited evaluation on external foundation policies: although motivated as a general plug-in strategy, the tactile adapter is only evaluated on top of the authors' own DiT policy rather than demonstrating plug-in capability on established open-source VLA models (such as OpenVLA or Octo).

Lack of multi-seed training variance: while Wilson confidence intervals are appropriately computed over the binomial real-robot trials, the variance induced by policy training seeds is not reported, which is particularly relevant when evaluating flow-matching and diffusion policies.

strengths: Extensive and rigorous real-world evaluation involving over 2,000 real-robot rollouts across four distinct bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks on an advanced hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with 6-DoF Inspire hands and 17 tactile pads per hand).

Well-motivated architecture design: decoupling visual tokens (joint self-attention with actions), proprioception/task condition (AdaLN modulation), and sparse tactile cues (dedicated cross-attention with LoRA adapter) is intuitive and empirically supported by the ablation experiments in Table 5.
Efficient adaptation paradigm: the plugin tactile adapter achieves performance comparable to full-scratch training (DECO.ds) while training only 7.97M parameters (<10% of total model capacity).

Valuable dataset contribution: DECO-50 provides 50 hours, 5M frames, and 8,000 trajectories of bimanual dexterous manipulation with synchronized active vision, proprioception, and dense tactile sensing.
weaknesses: Confounding architectural differences in baseline comparisons: As shown in Table 10, DECO uses a ResNet-34 visual backbone while ACT and DP/DP.t use ResNet-18, and DECO uses Flow Matching while DP uses DDIM. This makes it difficult to fully isolate whether the performance gain over DP stems solely from the decoupled DiT formulation or partly from the stronger visual encoder.

Baseline selection: The paper compares against standard visuomotor baselines (ACT and DP with simple input concatenation), but omits direct comparisons with other recently proposed visuo-tactile architectures mentioned in related work (e.g., ViTacFormer or slow-fast visuo-tactile fusion).

Minor typographic error in Table 4: The total row for DECO.p on the Assembly task is printed as '55/100', whereas each of the 4 sub-tasks has 20 trials (18+10+14+13 = 55/80), which also aligns with Table 1.

strengths: Substantial real-world robotic evaluation consisting of over 2,000 real robot rollouts across four diverse bimanual dexterous tasks on a dual-arm humanoid setup (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire dexterous hands).

Release of the DECO-50 dataset, which provides 50 hours, 5M frames, and 8,000 trajectories of bimanual dexterous teleoperation data equipped with high-resolution tactile sensing (1,062 contact points across 17 pads per hand) and active binocular vision.

A well-motivated and clean architectural design that decouples multimodal conditioning (joint self-attention for vision and actions, AdaLN for proprioception and diffusion timestep, and cross-attention for tactile cues), preventing cross-modal interference.

The plugin tactile adapter leverages LoRA and cross-attention to effectively adapt a frozen vision-based policy to contact-rich tasks while training fewer than 10% of the total model parameters, achieving competitive results to training from scratch.

Insightful empirical findings that clearly distinguish tasks where tactile feedback is critical (e.g., assembly and waste disposal) from tasks where vision and proprioception are sufficient (e.g., pick-and-place and sorting).
weaknesses: Asymmetry in baseline configurations: DECO utilizes a ResNet-34 visual backbone while ACT and DP employ ResNet-18, and DP's default U-Net channels were reduced. Although this was done to balance parameter counts, differences in visual backbone expressiveness complicate purely architectural comparisons.

The tactile encoder relies on relatively simple heuristics (pad-level spatial averaging concatenated with linear projections and a gated MLP); comparisons with learned self-supervised tactile representations or alternative spatial encodings are not explored.

Generalization and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation is relatively limited, with only three OOD objects evaluated on the sorting task (Table 12) and no formal OOD contact-rich assembly experiments.

strengths: Substantial real-world empirical evaluation: The paper conducts over 2,000 real-world rollouts across four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks on a complex dual-arm humanoid hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with 6-DOF Inspire dexterous hands).

Valuable multimodal dataset contribution: DECO-50 provides 50 hours, 8,000 successful trajectories, and over 5M frames of bimanual dexterous manipulation paired with active vision, proprioception, and multi-point tactile sensing across 17 pads per hand.

Well-motivated decoupled architecture and adapter design: Separating visual tokens (joint self-attention), proprioceptive states (AdaLN modulation), and sparse tactile signals (cross-attention + LoRA) provides an intuitive and parameter-efficient way (tuning under 10% of parameters) to augment pretrained vision-action models.

Clear task characterization: The experiments meaningfully differentiate between tasks where visual-proprioceptive cues suffice (pick-and-place, sorting) and contact-rich tasks where tactile feedback is critical (waste disposal, assembly).
weaknesses: Inconsistent baseline configurations: The proposed DECO architecture uses a ResNet-34 visual backbone, whereas baselines ACT and Diffusion Policy (DP) use ResNet-18, and DP uses a conditional U-Net with downscaled channels rather than a transformer-based diffusion backbone. A DiT-based baseline without decoupling or a standardized visual backbone across all methods would provide a fairer comparison.

Limited multimodal baseline comparisons: The only tactile baseline evaluated is DP.t (simple input concatenation to DP). The paper lacks comparisons against established visuo-tactile manipulation methods from the literature (e.g., slow-fast tactile fusion, ViTacFormer, or ACT with tactile tokens).

Discrepancies and typos in result tables: In Table 4, the total for DECO.p is printed as '55/100' instead of '55/80' (matching Table 1 and the 20-trial-per-category setup). In Table 3, DECO.p Stage 2 success is listed as 76/80, whereas Table 13 lists the total for Stage 2 as 72/80. Additionally, baseline evaluations on OOD objects in Table 12 are missing ('–/20').

Superficial treatment of tactile representation: The tactile encoder relies on simple per-pad averaging and linear projections. Given the 1,062 tactile contact points across both hands, there is little analysis of spatial taxel resolution, contact geometry, or temporal filtering of noisy sensor readings.

strengths: Extensive and rigorous real-world evaluation: The paper conducts over 2,000 real-robot rollouts across four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks on a full humanoid platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire dexterous hands), complete with stage-wise failure analyses and 95% Wilson confidence intervals.

Valuable dataset contribution (DECO-50): The collection of 50 hours, ~5M frames, and 8,000 successful trajectories of bimanual dexterous manipulation with high-density tactile sensor arrays (1,062 taxels per hand) and active binocular vision addresses a significant data gap in the tactile robotics community.

Parameter-efficient tactile adaptation: The two-stage training paradigm allows integrating tactile feedback via a dedicated cross-attention adapter and LoRA while tuning under 10% of total parameters, matching the performance of policies trained from scratch with tactile inputs (e.g., DECO.p vs. DECO.ds in Table 5).

Thorough ablations on modality routing: The ablation experiments effectively validate the proposed decoupled architecture, demonstrating that naive coupled conditioning (DECO.cs) fails to properly utilize touch and that swapping the injection pathways (Table 7) leads to catastrophic performance drops.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty: The individual architectural building blocks (MMDiT-style joint self-attention, AdaLN modulation, cross-attention for auxiliary tokens, and LoRA adaptation) are well-established primitives; the contribution is primarily an empirical and architectural integration rather than a novel learning methodology.

Mixed results on simulated tactile benchmarks: On the UniVTAC benchmark (Table 23), adding the tactile adapter yields no improvement over vision-only DECO (both achieving 82.1%), which weakens the general claim regarding the tactile adapter's efficacy across diverse setups and highlights potential domain or simulation-specific limitations.

Comparison with visuo-tactile baselines: In the real-world experiments, tactile comparisons are restricted to a naive concatenation baseline (DP.t) and internal ablations; comparisons against more sophisticated visuo-tactile fusion frameworks (e.g., slow-fast architectures or cross-modal representations like ViTacFormer/RDP) are missing in the hardware trials.

strengths: Extensive real-world robot evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across four diverse bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, complemented by evaluations on four established simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, and DexJoCo).

Principled and effective architectural design: the multimodal diffusion transformer explicitly decouples visual tokens (joint self-attention), proprioceptive state (AdaLN), and tactile feedback (cross-attention), aligning the injection pathway with each modality's structural and temporal properties.

Efficient and practical plugin tactile adapter: enables adapting a frozen vision-proprioception policy to contact-rich tasks by fine-tuning fewer than 10% of the total model parameters (7.97M out of ~91M) while matching the performance of training from scratch.
High-value robotic dataset contribution: DECO-50 supplies 50 hours (5M frames, ~8,000 successful trajectories) of bimanual dexterous teleoperation data with rich tactile sensing and active vision.
Insightful ablations, particularly verifying the necessity of specific pathway assignments (Table 7), showing catastrophic failure when swapping tactile and proprioceptive injection routes.
weaknesses: Hardware and sensor diversity is limited: physical experiments are restricted to a single embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) using piezoresistive normal pressure arrays, leaving cross-sensor transfer (e.g., to optical tactile sensors like GelSight or DIGIT) unvalidated.

Marginal tactile gains in simulated benchmarks: on UniVTAC (Table 23), DECO and DECO.p achieve identical average success rates (82.1%), indicating that the tactile adapter does not consistently provide advantages across all simulated setups.

Analysis of tactile representation remains largely empirical: the paper would benefit from deeper diagnostic insights or attention visualization explaining how the policy attends to specific tactile taxels during critical contact phases.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: parameter-efficient and effective integration of tactile feedback into visuomotor policies for bimanual dexterous manipulation.

The proposed decoupled architecture is well-principled and thoughtfully designed: vision and action tokens interact via joint self-attention, proprioceptive states and timestep embeddings are modulated via AdaLN, and tactile signals are injected via cross-attention with a lightweight LoRA-based adapter.
Extensive real-world robot evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across four distinct tasks on a complex platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP dexterous hands).
Release of the DECO-50 dataset (50 hours, 5M frames, 8K trajectories) provides a valuable public benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation with multi-taxel tactile sensing and active vision.

Insightful ablation experiments that justify design choices, specifically demonstrating the benefits of decoupled cross-attention versus coupled AdaLN conditioning for sparse tactile inputs (Table 5 and Table 7).
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons in the real-world experiments are primarily limited to ACT and standard Diffusion Policy (DP / DP.t), without benchmarking against other recent specialized visuo-tactile architectures (e.g., ViTacFormer or slow-fast visuo-tactile fusion models).

On the UniVTAC simulation benchmark (Table 23), DECO and DECO.p achieve identical average success rates (82.1%), indicating that the tactile adapter does not consistently improve performance across all visuo-tactile domains.

Real-world evaluations are restricted to a single hardware setup and a single sensor type (Inspire RH56DFTP piezoresistive array), leaving open the question of how well the adapter framework generalizes to optical tactile sensors (e.g., GelSight/DIGIT) or disparate hand morphologies.
